title: 14 Indian Cities Rank Among the World's Most Heat-Vulnerable. Here's What That Means for Your Family Back Home.
excerpt: A new Oxford University analysis of cities at greatest risk from extreme heat placed Nagpur, Chennai, Bengaluru, and 11 other Indian cities in the global top 50 — driven not just by soaring temperatures but by limited infrastructure, aging populations, and socioeconomic vulnerability.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • 14 Indian cities rank among the world's top 50 heat-vulnerable locations.
  • Extreme heat risks are compounded by socioeconomic vulnerability and poor infrastructure.
  • Indian workers may lose up to 22.5 working days annually due to heat.
  • Heatwaves significantly increase mental health hospitalizations, especially among the elderly.
  • Families should ensure cooling infrastructure and medical preparedness for loved ones.

Oxford University analysis
The next time you call your parents in Nagpur, Chennai, or Lucknow during the Indian summer, the conversation might need to go beyond "stay hydrated." A new global heat risk analysis led by Oxford University has ranked 14 Indian cities among the 50 most vulnerable to extreme heat worldwide — and the risks go far beyond discomfort. ## The Oxford Analysis Published this month, the study assessed cities with populations over one million across three dimensions: how extreme the heat exposure is, how vulnerable the population is (factoring in age, income, and health conditions), and how well the city can cope (access to air conditioning, tree cover, healthcare infrastructure). India, alongside Pakistan, Nigeria, and Ghana, hosts the largest number of cities in the at-risk top 50. The 14 Indian cities include: - **Maharashtra:** Nagpur, Pune - **Tamil Nadu:** Chennai, Madurai - **Uttar Pradesh:** Kanpur, Lucknow - **Karnataka:** Bengaluru - And seven other cities across multiple states "It isn't just exposure to hot temperatures that matters for risk," said lead author Nethmi Jayaratne Kariyawasam of Oxford. "Our study highlights the importance of multi-faceted global heat risk assessments, which reveal the diverse pathways through which urban heat risk emerges." > **"Even a single well-ventilated room can reduce heat-related health risks dramatically."** The critical insight: some cities that experience extreme heat — like Bangkok or Jeddah — ranked lower overall because their infrastructure and financial resources enable better coping. Indian cities often face the worst of both worlds — high exposure combined with limited adaptive capacity. ## The Health Toll A separate report by adelphi Global projects that Indian workers are set to lose **22.5 working days per year** due to extreme heat, with agriculture and construction workers bearing the brunt. India is likely to see 183 to 230 days annually with temperatures exceeding 30°C. ![Chennai — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/3/32/Chennai_Central.jpg) But the health consequences extend far beyond lost productivity. A study published in *Nature Health* in 2026 found that sustained extreme heat significantly increases mental health hospitalizations, particularly among older adults. Heatwaves disrupt sleep, destabilize medication regimens, and trigger acute episodes of anxiety and behavioral disorders. For the elderly — a demographic that skews disproportionately toward those "left behind" when younger family members migrate — these risks are compounded by isolation, limited mobility, and the inability to afford or access cooling.
The Impact of Extreme Heat

## Why the Diaspora Should Pay Attention For NRIs with aging parents in any of these 14 cities, the study is a practical call to action. Heat preparedness is not just about telling family to drink water — it requires thinking about: - **Cooling infrastructure:** Does your parents' home have functional air conditioning or at least access to a cooled common space? Even a single well-ventilated room can reduce heat-related health risks dramatically. - **Medical preparedness:** Heat interacts with common medications for blood pressure, diabetes, and mental health conditions. Families should review medication routines with a doctor before peak summer months. - **Check-in routines:** The combination of extreme heat and isolation is dangerous. Regular video calls during heat waves are not just comforting — they can be a literal early warning system for heat exhaustion or disorientation. - **Local support networks:** Community organizations, neighborhood associations, and even local temples and gurdwaras can serve as cooling centers and social safety nets. ## The Bigger Picture India's Meteorological Department announced it will develop a domestic heat impact index by next year, a step toward more granular, India-specific heat risk communication. But policy moves slowly, and individual families cannot wait for institutional change. The Oxford study's framework makes one thing clear: heat risk is not just about temperature. Cities where socioeconomic vulnerability and infrastructure gaps coincide with rising temperatures face a compounding crisis — and 14 Indian cities are already deep in that zone. For the diaspora, the question is no longer whether extreme heat is a problem. It is whether your family has a plan. **Sources:** Oxford University global heat risk study (July 2026); adelphi Global heat report; *Nature Health* (2026), Liu et al.; India Meteorological Department; The Hindu Business Line; Wall Street Journal; Reuters
